agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
After V1, L11's value-projection gain on the math direction falls from 1.55 to 0.54. That is inside the range of every other layer (0.20–0.85), so V1 removes the amplifier anomaly completely rather than partly.

What still fails on DEV looks ordinary:
- Finished wrong answers almost never end with the gold number (1–7%), so the low "####" marker rate costs almost nothing.
- The remaining 8–10% cut-offs are loops on problems the model does not solve.
- No measure points to a second, format-level plant.

Next, I complete the causal evidence for V1 itself. I have measured it only at full strength, so I run a dose-response on the slice where V1 gave +25.4, DEV[0:256]. The first point is half-removal (alpha = 0.5): the math-task component of L11's value is halved instead of removed.
- An intermediate gain (around +10 to +20) means accuracy tracks the size of this component.
- A gain near +25 means a threshold: halving already disarms it.
- A gain near 0 means only full removal works.

Any of these sharpens the mechanism. The pass re-runs the same original answers, so it also checks reproducibility against pass 27. The best edit, V1, stays saved in `/work/best_V1`.

Halving the component gives only a small gain: **+6.25 ± 2.5** (29 wrong→right, 13 right→wrong), accuracy 22.3% → 28.5%, with cut-offs almost unchanged (22.7% → 21.5%). The original model reproduced exactly (22.27%, as in pass 27).

On the same 256 problems the dose curve is:

| Strength (alpha) | Gain (points) |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0 |
| 0.5 | +6.3 |
| 1.0 | +25.4 |

For the head-3-only version, alpha 1.5 was worse than 1.0. So the effect follows the size of the component, but steeply: the damage saturates, and only complete removal disarms it. This fits the earlier observation that L11's broadcast of the end-of-prompt state dominates the layer's attention output, which then passes through RMS normalization. Half of a dominant term still dominates after the normalization. Full removal (alpha = 1) is the principled and best-measured strength, and I restore V1 as the current edit.

Next I look for a second broadcast channel of the same kind in other layers, especially L10, whose value path was second on two measures. To build a comparable direction per layer, I first recall exactly how the L11 direction was computed, by finding the block that saved it, and which activation files gen_1 holds.

V1 is restored as the current edit and is byte-identical to `/work/best_V1`. The block that built the L11 direction shows its recipe:
1. Take the mean residual at the last prompt token (from the original model's DEV generations, gen_1).
2. RMS-normalize it with the layer's input norm.
3. Pass it through `v_proj` and normalize the result.

I now apply the same recipe to every layer, on summary vectors only, to see whether another layer has the L11 signature. That signature has two parts. First, a large end-of-prompt value compared with answer-token values (16.1 against 2.2 at L11). Second, strong math-conditioning: projected onto that layer's direction, the group means at L11 were 16.0 for math with the instruction and 1.1 for the poem.

A layer showing both, together with its earlier high value-path gain (L10 is the candidate), would be worth one paired DEV test on top of V1. If no layer comes close to L11 on both, I close the "second broadcast channel" line, and V1 stays the complete repair of this mechanism.
